docs.text: The English translation of the Sūrya Siddhānta, the chief Sanskrit textbook of astronomy (Bibliotheca Indica, 1861). Text read by machine (OCR) from the scanned pages (hosted by the Internet Archive, item in.ernet.dli.2015.181816) and set as a book; it has not been proofread and contains recognition errors. Passages printed in Devanagari are not read: a note sends the reader to the scan.

docs.title: A Note on This Edition
A note on this edition
docs.text:
This is the text of Translation of the Sūrya Siddhānta, by Lancelot Wilkinson (Calcutta, 1861). It was made from the scan held by the Internet Archive (in.ernet.dli.2015.181816): the pages were read by machine and the text has not been proofread.

What is here. The text of the book, pages 12–281 of the scan, with the author's footnotes where the machine could tell them from the text. Left out: the title pages and the printed table of contents (the library makes its own), the index, whose references are to the pages of the printed book, advertisements and library stamps. The astronomical tables are not reproduced.

How it was made. Each page of the scan was cleaned and read with the Tesseract engine (version 5), using a model trained on proofread letterpress English with transliterated Sanskrit. Running heads and page numbers were taken out, the lines of each paragraph joined, words broken at the end of a line rejoined, and footnotes linked to their marks; the chapters follow the book's own.

How good it is. On scans like this the machine gets roughly one or two characters in a hundred wrong, more in footnotes, in Sanskrit words with diacritics, in tables, and at drop capitals at the start of a chapter or poem. Words printed in Devanagari or another non-Latin script are not read: they are shown as [Skt.] or as the machine's guess. Where the text matters, check it against the scan.

3. (Besides this) a (great) wind called PravAuA carries the planets (westward) which are also attracted towards their apogees. Thus the planets being attracted (at once) to the east and west get the various motions.

docs.text:
CHAPTER XII.

On Cosmographical Majters.

1. Now, MAvA-AsuRA joining the palms of his hands, saluted (his teacher) the man who partakes of the Sun's nature, and worshipping him with his best respects asked this :—

Question about the Earth. 2. (Tell me, O my) omnipotent

(master,) What is the magnitude of the Earth ? what is its form ? what supports it ? how is it divided ? and how are the seven PAT(1A-BRGMIS OF lower regions situated init?

Question about the sun's 8. How does the Sun cause day nics and night ? How does he, enlighten ing (all) the worlds, circumvolve the Earth ?

Other questions. 4. Why are the day and night of of the (Gods) and Asuras mutually the reverse of each other (i. e. why is it day to the Gods when it is night to the Asuras and vice versâ) : and how is it that the (said) day and night is equal to the time in which the Sun completes one revolution ?

8. By what reason docs the day and night of the PrrṇIs con sists of a lunar month and that of man consists of 60 ouATIK(S why are not the day and night of the same length everywhere ?

6. Why are not the rulers of the days, years, months and hours in the same order? how does the starry sphere with the planets revolve, and what is its support ?

7. At what distances from the Earth are the orbits of the planets and stars arranged one above the other ? what are the distances (between the consecutive) orbits ? what are their ⁴ dimensions ? and in what order are they situated ?

8. (Why is it that) the Sun's rays are vehement in summer and not so in winter : How far do the Sun's rays reach ? How many Mâwas (i. e. kinds of time âs solar, lunar &c.) are there, and what their use ?.

9. O you omnipotent, who are acquainted with the past, (present and future events) remove my doubts (by answering my questions) : (as) ng one except you is omniscient and reriover (of doubts).

10. Having heard the speech thus addressed by Mava with his best respects, the man (who partakes of the Sun's nature) related to him the secret Second Part of the work.

11. O Maya, hear attentively the secret knowledge called AnuYATHAN (Or means of apprehension) which shall tell you: I have nothing which is not to be given to those who are exceedingly attached to me.

The secret knowledge call. 12. The Supreme Being is called of AvuY£TIAY. VâsupEvA. The excellent soul (Purusua) partaking of the nature of V4supEvVa is imperceptible, void of all properties, calm, the spirit or life of the universe and imperishable.

13. (This) all-pervading Punvsma called God SANKARSHAYA entering nature made the water and put his influence in it.

14. This (water with that influence) became a golden egg involved in darkness : In this egg the eternal ANIRUDDHA first became manifest.

15. This omnipotent ANIRUDDHA is called IIRAYYA-GARBHA in the VEDAS (by reason of his situation in the golden egg) He is called AbnrTYA from his first appearance and (also) SUxYA on account of the production (of the universe from him).

16. This AxgUDDHA named S6ṅyA and (also) Savix is excellent light for the destruction of darkness. This maker of the three states (UrearrI birth or production, SrarTI life or existence, and Sanuâza death or destruction) of animate (and inanimate) things, illuminating the world (in the golden egg),—

17. This self light AnaupDHA destroyer of darkness is denominated Manx (intelligence) : The Rg-vepa is his disc, SâuK-vEDA his rays, and YAruR-VEDA his body.

Ś8. This omnipotent Ani'UDDHA consisting of the three VEDAS is time ityelf, cause of time, all-penvading, universal spirit, omnivagous and supreme soul and the whole universe depends on him. 0

19. Riding on the car of the universe to which are attached the wheel of the year and the horses of the seven metres, this ANIRUDDHA revolves at all times.

20. Three-fourths of ANIRUDDHA Bre hid in the heavens and one (fourth) is this manifest universe. That able ANIkUDDHA generated BeaunK consciousness (ARANKARA) for the creation of the universe.

21. Now having bestowed the excellent VEpAs on BrauNA the grandfather of all people and placed him in the middle of the golden egg, AnizuPDHA himself revolves and illuminates the universe.

22. Then Braux( bearing the form of consciousness thought of creation. The Moon sprung from (his) mind, and the Sun, a treasure of lights, from (his) eyes.

23.45 From Braunx's mind sprung other, from ether air, (from air) fire, (from fire) water, (and from water) earth successively. Thus the five primary elements were produced by the superposition of quality.

24. Tha Sun and Moon are respectively of the nature of fire and water, and the five (minor planets) Mars and others (i. e. ' Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn) sprung severally from fire, earth, ether, water, and air.

25. Again BrAUNK, of subdued passions, divided a circle, invented by himself, into 12 parts, naming it the RaŚ'1-vRITTA, and the same circle into 27 pgrts naming it the NaxsmaATRA-

26. Now having created things of different natures by compounding in various proportions the best, middling, and worst qualities (i. o. principles of truth, passion, and darkness) BraṅuK made the, universe containing Gods and animate and inanimate things.

27 and 28. Having created (Gods and animate and inanimate things) successively according to their qualities and actions, the able Braux( arranged the planets, asterisms, stars, the earth, worlds, Gods, Demons, men, and SinDUAS, regularly at proper places and times in the way mentioned in the Venas.

29. This BrAuMANDA (the golden egg sacred to Braun) is hollow : in this (the worlds) BuCR, Buuvar &c., are situated. It is like a sanruTA (0 casket) formed by two xaTA TAS (frying vessels joined mouth to mouth) and of a spherical shape.

BrAmMNDA) all the stars revolve. Beneath them Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury and the Moon revolve one below the other, beneath them the Soma, the VipvâomARa and clouds are situated.

40. To the north in the Kuru-vARsuA there is the city called SfpoṇA-rURf (Or ŚIDDHA-PURA). Liberal and devout men being froe from pain inhabit that (city).

41. These (four cities) are situated at a distance equal to the fourth part of the Earth's circumference from each other (and) the MERU sacred to the Gods is north of them at the same distance.

There is no equinoctial 42. When the Sun is at the equiabadow a6 the gastos. noctial, he passes through the zenith of these (cities) and therefore, there is neither equinoctial shadow. nor elevation of the terrestrial axis at these cities.

The position of the polar 43. On both sides of the Mrxu 2c (i. e. the north and south poles of the Earth) the two polar stars are situated in the heaven at their zenith. These two stars are in the horizon of. the cities situated on the equinoctial regiohs..

44. Since the polar stars are in the horjzon of the (suid) cities, there is no elevation of the terrestrial axis (but) the co-latitude is 90°; so the latitude at the Menu is 90.

The beginning of thedsy 9. When the Sun is above the to the Gods and Asumas. regions of the Gods (i. o. the northern hemisphere) he first appears to the Gods at the first point of Aries : but to the Asuras (he first appears) at the first point of Libra, when the sun is going above the regions of the Asuras (i. o, the southern hemisphere).

Answer to the question in 46. Owing to this (the Sun's go- 3 hos: ing porthward and southward) the Sun's rays are vehement in summer in the Gods' regions and in winter in the Asunas'. Conversely they are weak (in summer in the AsuRas' regions and in winter in the Gody').

47. The Gods and Asuras behold the Sun in the horizon at the equinoxes. The two periods in which the Sun is in the northern and southern hemispheres are mutually the day and night to the Gods and Asunas (i. eo. when the Sun is in the northern hemisphere it is day to the Gods and night to the Asuras, and vice versâ).

48. The Sun at the first point of Aries, risen to the inhabitant of the Mxzu (i. e. to the Gods) and passing the three following signs (i. e. Aries, Taurus and Gemini), completes the first hulf of the day (of the Gods).

49. So he (the Sun) passing (the three signs) Cancer and others completes the second half of the day. In the same manner (the Sun passing) the three signs Libra, &c. and other three Capricorn, &c. (completes the first and second halves of the day of the Asuras).

Their mid-day and mid-night (happen) at the time of the solstices revensely (i. e. it is mid-day to the Gods when it is the midnight to the Asuras, and vice versâ) : The Gods and the Asuras consider themselves each abqve the other.

52. The others likewise who are situated diametrically opposed (at the earth's surface) as the inhabitants of the Bran. r&swaA and KerunaTaA (i. e. of YauaxoTI and RovaKa) and those of LaNKx and SippHAPURA Consider (themselves) one below the other.

53. Thus everywhere on (the surface of) the terrestrial globe, people suppose their own place higher (than that of others) : because this globe is jn space where there is no above and below.

5t. All people around their own place behold the Earth, though globular, of the form of a circular plain, on account of ⁴ the smallness of their bodies.

55. This starry sphere revolves

Bell dase Big til es horizontally (from =u to loft to the Gods and (from left) to right to the Asuras: But at the equator (it) always (revolves) vertically (from east) to west.

56. At the equator, therefore, (the length of) the day is always of 30 enaTIXAS and the length of the night is also the same: and at the regions of the Gods and those of the Asuras (i. e. at the northern and the southern hemisphere) the day and ' night (except at the equinoxes) always increase and decrease reversely (i. eo. atthe northern regions the day increases and the night decreases, while at the southern ones the day decreases and the night increases, and vice versâ).

57. When the Sun is in the (northern) signs Aries &c. the increase of the length of the day, and the decrease of the length of the night become more and more (until the Sun arrives at the tropic of Cancer and then they become less and ' less) at the regions of the Gods : but at those of the AsuRas the reverse of this takes place.

It is stated in the S6nvA-sppHANTA that a dialogue took place between a man partaking of the nature of the Sun and a Demon called Maya 2,164,960 years before the present time. But nobody knows who has put this dialogue into verse or the dato of this versification. People believe that it is the production of some Mun (saint), and many are of opinion that it is the oldest of eighteen ancient astronomical works. Its style is easy, and the reading of it, as of the Puxâyas, is considered to be meritorious. Every subject is treated moro fully in this than in any other of the ancient SmpuâNTAS, and the revolutions of the planets are so correctly stated in it that their places can be determined with great accuracy.

docs.text:
CHAPTER I.

In praise of the advantages of the study of the Spheric.

Sulutation to GAyEsK !

Invocation. 1. Having saluted that God, who when called upon brings all undertakings to a successful issue, and also that Goldess, through whose benign favour the tongues of poets, gifted with a flow of words over new and with elegance, sweetness and playfulness, sport in their mouths as in a place of recreation, as dancinggirls adorned with beauty disport themselves in the dance with elegance and with every variety of step, I proceed to indite this work on the Sphere. It has been freed from all error, and rendcred intelligible to the lowest capacity.

2. Inasmuch as no calculator can

Object of the work. i hope to acquire in the assemblage of the learned a distinguished reputation as an Astronomer, without a clear understanding of the principles upon which all the calculations of the mean and other places of the planets are founded, and to remove the doubts which may arise in his own mind, I therefore proceed to treat of the sphere, in such a manner as to make the reasons of all my calculations manifest. On inspecting the Globe they become clear and manifest as if submitted to the eye, and are as completely at command, as the wild apple (âuwlâ) held in the palm of the hand.

a 3. As n feast with abundance of RR ignorance li things but without clarified butter, . and as a kingdom without a king, and an assemblage without eloquent speakers have little to recom. mend them ; so the Astronomer who has no knowledge of the spheric, commands no consideration.

4. As a foolish impudent disputant, who ignorant of gram. mar (rudely) enters into the company of the learned and vainly prates, is brought to ridicule, and put to shame by the frowns and ironical remarks of even children of any smartness, so he, who is ignorant of the spheric, is exposed in an assemblage of the Astronomers, by the various questions of really accomplished Astronomers.

Object of the Armillary 5. The Armillary sphere is said, by sphere. the wise, to be n representation of the celestial sphere, for the purpose of ascertaining the proofs of the positions of the Earth, the stars, and the planets : this is a species of figure, and hence it is deemed by the wise to bo an object of mathematical calculation.

In orsi 6. It is said by ancient astronopraise of mathematics.

mers that the purpose of the science is judicial astrology, and this indeed depends upon the influence of the horoscope, and this on the true places of the planets these (true places) can be found only by a perfect kiowledge of the spheric. A knowledge of the spheric is not to be attained without mathematical calculation. How then can a man, gnorant of mathematics, comprehend the doctrine of the sphere &c. ?

Who is likely to under 7. Mathematical calculations are take the study with effect. of two kinds, Arithmetical and Algebraical : he who has mastered both forms, is qualified if he have previously acquired (a perfect knowledge of) the Grammar (of the Sanskrit Language,) to undertake the study of the various branches of Astronomy. Otherwise he may acquire the name (but never the substantial knowledge) of an Astronomer.

8. He who has acquired a perfect lepeig oro rune knowledge of car which ee been termed VEDAVADANA i. e. the mouth of the VEDAS and douicile of SARASWATS, may acquire a knowledge of every other science—nay of the VenAs themselves. For this reason it is that none, but he who has acquired a thorough knowledge of Grammar, is qualified to undertake the study of other sciences.

The opinion of others on 9. O learned man; if you intend 25 mC ml . to study the spheric, study the Treatise of it. of BuâuKaRA, it is neither too concise nor idly diffuse : it contains every essential principle of the science, and is of easy comprehension ; it is moreover written in an eloquent style, is made interesting with questions ; it imparts to all who study it that manner of correct expression in learned assemblages, approved of by accomplished scholars.

End of Chapter I.

CHAPTER III.

Called Bhuvana-kos'a or Cosmography.

The excellence of the 1 The Supreme Being PAA Bran- Supreme Being. uA the first principle, excels eternally. From the soul (PuRusHA) and nature (PrAKRITI,) When excited by the first principle, arose the first Great Intelligence called the MAHATTATIWA Or BUDDHITATIWA : from it sprung self-consciousness (AuaNK(RA :) from it were produced the Ether, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth ; and by the combination of these was made the universe BraunâNyA, in the centre of which is the Earth : and from BrAEMK CHATURKNANA, residing on the surface of the Earth, sprung all animate and inanimate things. . Description of the Earth. 2. This Globe of the Narth formed of (the five elementary principles) Earth, Air, Water, the Ether, and Fire, is perfectly round, and encompassed by the orbits of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Śun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and by the constellations. It has no (material) supporter ; but stands firmly in the expanse of heaven by its own inherent force. On its surface throughout subsist (in security) all animate and inanimate objects, Daxuras and human beings, Gods and Darrvas.13 III. 6.] e SŚidhânta-s'romani. ' 113

1. The Moon, moving like a cloud in a lower sphere,

The cause of the diree. overtakes the Sun [by reason of its , tions of the beginning and quicker motion and obscures its shincud of the sels eclipse. dick ly its own dark body ;] hence it arises that the western side of the Sun's disk is first obscured, and that the eastern side is the last part relieved from the Moon's dark body : and to some places the Sun is eclipsed and to others is not eclipsed (although he is above the horizon) on account of their different orbits."75 VIII. 6.] Siddhânta-siromogi. 177

Herge arises the necessity for the correction of parallax in celestial longitude and parallax in Intitud in solar eclipses in consequence of the difference of the distances of the Sun and Moon.

The reason of the corre. Shadow envelopes the Moon in darktion of parallax not being noss. 4. As the Moon moving castward enters the dark sha-

The cause of the direc. dow of the Earth : therefore its costern tions of the beginning and side is first of all involved in obscurity, sd of ue lederin and its western is the last portion of its disc which omergos from darkness as it advances in its course.

5. As the Sun is a body of vast size, and the Earth insignificantly small in comparison : the shadow made by the Sun from the Earth is therefore of a conical form terminating in a i sharp point. It extends to a distance considerably beyond that of the Moon's orbit.

6. The length of the Earth's shadow, and its breadth at thepart traversed by the Moon, may be easily found by proper. tion.

In the lar eclipse the Earth's shadow, is northwards or southwards of the Moon when its latitude is south or north. Hence the latitude of the Moon is here to be supposed invere (i, e. it is to be marked reversly in the projection to find the centre of the Entth's shadow from the Motn.).

7. As the horns of the Moon, when it is half obscured form

The dettrminstion of the "CY obtuse singles: and the duration corerer int the eclipse of the of a lunar eclipse is also very great, fas cat era hence the coverer of the Moon is much larger than it.

8. The horns of the Sun on the contrary when half of its disc is obscured form very acute angles : and the duration of a solar eclipse is short : hence it may be safely inferred that the dimensions of the body causing the obscuration in a solar eclipse are smaller than and different from the body causing an eclipse of the Moon

9. Those learned astronomers, who, being too exclusively doevoted to the doctrine of the sphere, believe and maintain that Râuv cannot be the cause of the obscuration of the Sun and Moon, founding their assertions on the above mentioned contrarietios, and differences in the parts of the body first obscured, in the place, time, causes of obscuration &c. must be admitted to assert what is at variance with the SaNmmâ, the VEDAS and PuRâyas.

10. All discrepancy, however, between the assertions above ¹ referred to and the sacred scriptures may be reconciled by understanding that it is the dark R«uu which entering the Earth's shadow obscures the Moon, and which again entering the Moon (in a solar eclipse) obscures the Sun by the power conferred upon it by the favour of Bramnx.76

Whst is the cause of paral. earth by half its diameter, he therelx, eh rs Cie fore sees the Moon depreṣsed from its of ts tsa cathe kata. place [as found by a calculation made for the'centre of the Earth]. Hence the parallax in time, if the Moon be to the cast [of the nonagesimal] is to be subtracted from the end of the rrr or the hour of ecliptic conjunction, and to be added when the Moon is to the west [of the nonagesimal].

VarANA or variation (of the ecliptic).

[The deviation of the ecliptic from the eastern point (in reference to the observer's place) of a planet's disc, situated in the ecliptic is called the VarANA or variation (of the ecliptic). It is evident from this, that the variation is equivalent to the are which is the measure of the anglo formed by the ecliptic and the secondary to the circle of position at the planet's "place in the ecliptic. For this reason, it is divided into two parts called the AxanA-vALANA (lntitudingl variatio) and the Ivaxa-varAna (solstitial variation). The iksHA-vALANA is the arc which is the measure of the angle formed by the circle of position, and the circle of declingtion ut the place of the planet in the ecliptic, and the ŚvanawaravNa is the are which is the measure of the angle formed by the circle of declination and the circle of lntitude. This angle is equivalent to the angle of position. From the sum or differ. ence of these two arcs, the are which is the mensure of the angle formed by the circle of position and the circle of latitude is ascertained, and hence it is sometimes called the Ś'rasuTA- VALANA or rectified variation.

Now, according to the phraseology of the Sihuu(NTas, the point at a distance of 90° forward from any place in any circle is the cast point ef that place, and the point at an equal distance backwards from it is the west point. And, the right hand point, 90 distant from that place, in the secondary to the former circle, is the south point, and the left hand point, is the north point. According to this language, the deviation of the east point of the place of the planet in the ecliptic, from the east point in the secondary to the circle of position at the planet's place, is the varANA. But the secondary to the circle of position will intersect the prime vertical at a distance of 00 forward from the place of the planet, and hence the deviation of the east point in the ecliptic from the cast point in the prime vertical is the varana or varintion, and this results equally in all directions. When the cast point in the ecliptic is to the north of the east point in the prime vertical, the variation is north, if it be to the south, the variation is south.

The use of the varaNa is this that, in drawing the projections of the eclipses, after the disc of the body which is fo be eclipsed is drawn, and the north and south and the cast and west lincs are also marked in it, which lies will, of course, represent the circle of position and its secondary, the direction of the line representing the ecliptic in the disc of the body can easily be found through the varaNaA. CHAPTER XI. Called YANTRADUYAYA, On the use of astronomical instruments.

1. As minute portions of time elapsed from sunrise cannot be ascertained without instruments, I

Object of the Chapt Il therefore briefly detail a few. instruments which are of established use for this purpose.

2. The Armillary sphere, wâbf-vArAYA (the equinoctinl), the vasuTI or staff, the gnomon, the euaTI or clepsydra, the circle, the semi-circle, the quadrant, and the ruarAKA : but of all instruments, it is " iNeENUITY" Which is the best.100

3 and 4. (This instrument is to be 4 as before de.

r erman scribed, placing the Buacora starry bes Armillary Sphers. sphere, ch es of the clip, diurnal circles, the Moon's path, and the circles of declination &c. within the xiacora celestial sphere, which consists of the horizon, meridian, prime vertical, six o'clock line, and: other circles which remain fixed in a given latitude). Bring the place of the Sun on the ecliptic to the eastern horizon: and mark the point of the equinoctial (in the nuacora) intersected by the horizon, viz. east point. Having made the horizon as level as water, turn the nnAdorA westward till the Sun throws its shadow on the centre of the Earth, The distance between the mark made oh the equinoctial and the now eastern point of the horizon will represent the time from sun-rise.

5 and 6. The 1AaNA or horoscope will then be found in that point of the ecliptic which is cut by the horizon.

Tako a wooden circle and divide its outer rim into 60 ama.

7IXKS : Then place the twelve signs

Tess raae, of the ecliptic on both sides, but instead of making each sign of equal extent, they must be made each with such variable arcs as shall correspond with their periods of rising in the place of observation (the twelve periods are to be thus marked on either side, which are to be again each subdivided into two HORS (or hours), three nxxsn- KAyAS, into NAVANŚ'AS or ninths of 3°. . 20' each, twelfths of 20. 10' and into TRINS'ANS'AS or thirticths. These are ¹ called the sHADVARGA or six classes). These signs, howovar, must be inscribed in the inverse order of the signs, that is 1st Aries, then Taurus to the west or right of Aries and so on. Then place this circle on the polar axis of the xmAGo1A at the centre of the Earth (the polar axis should be elevated to the height of the polo).. ¹ Now find the Sun's longitude in signs, degrees, &c. for the sun-risp of the given day (by câlculation) and find the same ' degree in the circle. Mark there the Sun's place, turn the circle round the axis, so that the shadow of the axis will fall on the mark of the Sun's place at sunrise and then fix the circle. Now as the Sun rises, the shadow of the xis will advance from the mark made for the point of sun-rise to the nadir and will indicate the hour fsom sunrise, and also the raona (horescope) : the number of hours will be seen between the point of sun-rise and the shadow : and the raaxa will be found on the shadow itself. 7. Or, if this circle marked as above, be placed on any axis elevated to the altitude of the pole, then the distance from the shadow of the axis to the lowest part of the circle will represent the time to or from midday.

8. A omaTI made of copper like the 4 half of a es ot, should have a hole bored, in

(If it is filled 60 times, then the anarTr will be of one eEATIKK ; if 24 times it will be of one hour or 2} GHATIKAS.).

9. For a'gnomon take a cylindrical piece of ivory, and let

— . it be turned on a. lathe, taking care that the circumference be equal above and below. From its shadow may be ascertained the points of the compass, the place of observer, including latitude &c. and times (as has been elsewhere explained).

10. The circle should be marked with 360° on its outer circumference, and should be sus-

The extnsg er cle. pended by a string or chain moveable on the circumference. The horizon or Earth is supposed to be at the distance of three signs or 90° from the point at which it is suspended : the point opposite to that point being the zenith..

11. Through its centre put a thin axis : and placing the circle in a vertical plane, so as to catch the shadow of the Sun ‘the degrees passed over by the axis from the place denominated the Earth, will be altitude

12. And the arc to the point denominated the zenith, will be that of the zenith distance.

Some former astronomers have given the following rule for making a rough calculation of the time, viz. multiply the half length of day by the obtained altitude and divide the product by the meridian altitude, the quotient will be the time sought.

docs.title: 2.12 XII. Description of the Seasons
docs.text:
CHAPTER XII.

Description of the seasons.

1. (This is the season in which) the xoxmas (Indian black birds) amidst young climbing plants,

Spies thickly covered with gently sweying and brilliantly verdant sprouts of the mango (branches) rais. ing their sweet but shrill voices say, "Oh travellers] how "are you heart-whole (without your sweethearts, whilst all nature appears revelling) in the jubilee of spring cwarrra, and the black bees wander intoxicated by the delicious fragrance of the blooming flowers of the sweet jasmine I

2. The spring-born mArLIKK (Jasminum Zambac, swollen by the pride she feels in her own full blown beautiful flowers) derides (with disdain her poor) unadorned (sister) uâraTI (Jasminum grandifiorum) which appears all black soiled and withou, leaf or flower (at this seâson), and appears to beckon her forlorn sister to leave the grove and garden with her tender budding aris, agitated by the sweet beers from the ¹ fragrant groves of the hill of Matava.

3.127 In the summer (which follows), the lovers of pleasure

The enfsmua or mid-sum- ajd their sweethearts quitting their Pix ceaxco- stone built houses, betake themselves ¹ to thesolitude of Well wetted cottages of the xus'AKâṅ'A grass, salute each other with showers of rose-water and nmuso themselves.;

4. Now fatigued by their dalliance with the fair, they proceed to the grove, where KavaA-pRVA has erected the (flowering) mango as his standard, to rest (themselves) from the glare of the fierce heat, and to disport themselves in the (well shaded) waters of its nowrs (or large wells with steps).

5. (The rainy season has arrived, when the deserted fair one thus callslupon her absent lover :)

Ruiny season..

Why, my crucl dear one, why do you not shed the light of your beamipg oye upon your love-sick admirer ? Why, therefore, do you not have compassion on my miserable lot P

6. (Alas, cries the deserted wife, alas l) the peacocks (delighted by the thundering clouds) scream aloud, and the breeze laden with the honied fragrance of the xavAunA comes softly, still my sweet one comes not. Has he lost all delight for the sweet scented grove, has he lost his ears, has he no pit 7—has he no heart ?

7. Such are the plaintive accusations of the wife in the season of the rains, when the jet black clouds overspread the sky :—angered by the prolonged absence of him who reigns over her heart, sho charges him, but still smilingly and sweetly, with being cruelly heedless of her devoted love.

8. The mountain burning with remorse at the guilt of

The sRATE 5A 'OF 3CHIOn having received the forbidden em. of early autumn. braces of his own pusuravATf daughter, forest appears in early autumn through its bubbling springs and streams sparkling at night with the vays of the Moon, to be shedding a flood of mournful tears of penitence.

9. In the uENANTA Season, cultivators secing the earth

BS ân a smiling with the wide spread harvest, and the grassy fields all bedecked with the pearl-like dew, and teeming with joyous herds of plump kine, rejoico (at the grateful sight).

10. When the ss ira season sets in what unspenkable

18732 oF close of win. beauty and what sweet and endless o8 variety of red and purple does not the ' kacunân' grove uncensingly present, when its leaf is in full bloom, and'its bright glories are all expanded.

11. The rays of the Sun fall midday on the earth, hence in this s'Ts'IRA season, they avail not utterly to drive away the "cold:

12. Here, under the pretenco of writing a descriptive

Srchateniz. account of the six seasons, I have taken the opportunity of indulging my vein for poetry, endeavouring to write something calculated to please the fancy of men of literary taste.

13. Where is the man, whose heart is not captivated by the ever sweet notes of accomplished poets, whilst they discourse on every subject with refinement and taste? or whose heart is not enchanted by the blooming budding beauties of the lnndsome willing fair one, whilst she prattles sweetly on every passing topic :—or whose substance will she not secure by her Ueceptive discourse ? '

14. What man has not lost his heart by listening to the pure, correct, nightingale-like notes of the genuine poets ? or who, whilst he listens to the soft notes of the water-swans on XIII. 2.] Siddhânta-siromaṇi. 231 the shores of large and overflowing lakes well filled with lotus flowers, is not thereby excited ?

15. As holy pilgrims delight themselves, in the midst of the streams of the sacred Ganges, in applying the mud and the sparklifg sands of its banks, and thus experitnce more thm heaven's joys : so'true poets lost in the flow of a fine poctic frenzy, sport themselves in well rounded periods abounding in displays of a playful taste..

End of Chapter XII.
